claim: Institutions now operate under a guardrail that they may welcome identity content but cannot let race itself tip the decision. Harvard's official guidance: 'applicants and those writing on behalf of applicants should feel welcome to write about any aspect of the applicant's identity or background, including race and/or ethnicity,' while the demographic race/ethnicity data 'will not be shared in the transmission of application data for review.' The essay's narrative reaches the reader; the bare category is withheld. The carve-out is the only legitimate channel through which an applicant's race can inform a decision.

application.content: Treat the essay as the only place racial identity can actually do work in the file — but only in its qualitative, experience-tied form, never as a checkbox the reader will weight. Practical consequence: if a student wants their background to matter, it must be EARNED in narrative (a specific experience evidencing a quality), because the demographic checkbox is redacted before the reader sees it. Don't spend the essay restating what a (withheld) box would have said; spend it on what only a story can convey.

Warning sign that a student is mis-modeling the new system: a draft that 'reports' identity for the record (as if confirming a demographic) rather than dramatizing it. Under redaction, reportage is invisible; only the lived, transferable quality survives. Redirect the student from 'telling the reader what I am' to 'showing the reader who that made me and what I'll bring.'

sources.citation: Harvard College Admissions official FAQ — 'Can I (as an applicant) write about my race/ethnicity in my application materials?'

Stanford Center for Racial Justice SFFA FAQ — colleges may consider how race shaped a personal journey but must treat the student 'based on his or her experiences as an individual—not on the basis of race,' and may not use essays to restore race-conscious admissions

connections.note: Data-redaction is the operational answer to the ruling's anti-circumvention warning.
The carve-out is what makes essay-borne identity admissible at all once the checkbox is withheld.

provenanceTrail: Harvard's institutional FAQ (Tier 1) fetched directly and quoted verbatim for the 'feel welcome to write about... including race and/or ethnicity' and 'will not be shared in the transmission' language. Cross-checked against Stanford Law's FAQ describing the same can/cannot boundary at the system level. The two sources are independent (one institutional, one legal-academic) and agree.
